title: Empty the Mind
hook: Your head is not public seating; every loose screen you allow keeps a chair for noise.
counterintuition: Trying to crush a thought often feeds it. The quieter move is to sort it: controllable, uncontrollable, or just fresh noise from the room.
tryThisNow: Move one feed, app, or screen out of first reach, then compare two places it could live and choose the one that makes useless replay harder.
keyTakeaway: A clear mind is not blank; it sorts each loop by control, cuts fresh input at the door, and returns attention to the next thing you can do now.

breakdown.fastRead: At a sports bar dinner, a dozen televisions tug at every booth. A friend is telling a story, but the eyes keep moving to scores, ads, and news crawls. The room is doing part of the thinking for you. Then the mind copies the room. It keeps replaying old arguments, fake futures, and clips you never chose. Mental clearing means removing those loops so attention can return to what you can govern. Epictetus gave the sharp test: controllable or uncontrollable. If a thought cannot lead to conduct, it does not get the chair.
breakdown.deepRead:
Epictetus gives the mind a sorting tray: controllable on one side, uncontrollable on the other. The list is not meant to sound grand. It is meant to stop a loop before it spends the afternoon in your head. Weather, other people's moods, the old comment in the meeting, and tomorrow's outcome do not take orders from you. Your attention, judgment, next word, and next act do.

Brooke sees the same pattern at home after the sports bar. She wanted a quiet dinner, but the wall of televisions taught her eyes to keep grazing. Later, while brushing her teeth, she catches herself replaying headlines she did not care about and an argument she has not had. The screen is gone, but the feed is still running inside. She writes two columns on a receipt: can govern, cannot govern. In the first column she puts apologize, close the app, ask one clear question. In the second she puts someone else's tone, market news, old embarrassment. A clear mind is a workbench, not a vacant lot. It has room for the tool in your hand because the wrong tools are back on the shelf.

The move is gentle, but it is not vague. Name the loop. Sort it by control. Return to conduct. If the thought shows you a duty, take the next small step. If it only rehearses fear, do not feed it with another lap.
breakdown.fullRead:
Hermine sits in a radiology reading room with six studies left in the queue. The room is dim, the monitors are bright, and a side screen keeps flashing sports highlights from the waiting area. Nothing loud is happening. Still, her notes show three pauses in ten minutes, each one after a score update. The first lesson is plain: a quiet body can still live in a noisy room.

The harder lesson starts after the side screen is off. A headline can leave. A grudge can stay. So can a fantasy about proving someone wrong, or a fear that asks for the same answer every hour. Those loops feel like work because they use effort. They are not work unless they change a word, a choice, or a duty. Epictetus's split helps here because it gives the mind a firm place to stop. Other people's reactions go in the outside pile. Your judgment of the next right act stays in your hands.

This does not mean pushing thoughts into a basement. Suppression gives the thought a wrestling partner. Anyone who has tried not to think about a bad email knows the trick. The email grows teeth. Mental clearing works better when it gives the thought a fair hearing, then asks for its claim. Is there a repair to make? Make it. Is there a fact to check? Check it. Is there only a movie of disaster, revenge, or praise? Let it pass without buying another ticket.

The edge case is real pain. A loss, a diagnosis, a debt notice, or a hard talk at home cannot be sorted away like a pop-up ad. Stillness is not a refusal to care. It is a refusal to let care become useless rehearsal. If the grief needs a call, make the call. If the bill needs a plan, write the first line. If the outcome is no longer yours, do not spend the night pretending your worry is a lever.

Environment still matters. You can be strong and still choose a quieter table. You can care about the world and still remove the news widget from the first screen you see. The sports bar televisions are a warning, not because televisions are evil, but because the mind learns from what the room repeats. Give the room fewer hooks, then give the mind a clear test. Controllable gets action. Uncontrollable gets released from duty.

A clear mind is not blank. It sees more because fewer voices are shouting over the evidence. It notices the person across the table. It hears the sentence under the anger. It spots the small next step that rumination hid. The empty space is not waste. It is where choice can stand.

examples.title: Map Noise Split

planSpec.domain: late transit after a noisy dinner
planSpec.audience: commuters carrying input noise into the next choice
planSpec.stakes: One person keeps feeding attention with screens while another sorts what can be acted on.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Two people face the same platform noise and diverge by sorting control differently.

examples.scenario: Aanya studies the subway platform map after a sports bar dinner under televisions while the overhead screen cycles delays and headlines. She keeps opening the news feed, then loses the route she just found. Ludovic traces one line with his finger, names the delay uncontrollable, and chooses the platform he can reach. The same noise pulls one of them back into the room and sends the other toward the train.
examples.whatToDo: Aanya closes the feed and asks Ludovic to read the map aloud once. They sort delay from action, then walk to the reachable platform without checking the screen again.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast shows how attention follows the last input unless someone interrupts it. Sorting control turns the same bad delay into a usable next step.

examples.title: Weather Is Not a Task

planSpec.audience: workers stuck rehearsing an outcome they cannot govern
planSpec.stakes: A crew can waste its prep time fearing weather instead of protecting seedlings.
planSpec.requiredBeat: A mentor reframes a stuck view with a quotable control sentence.

examples.scenario: Brooke sorts saplings on a tree nursery table with three weather alerts buzzing in her pocket. She keeps saying the frost will ruin the whole week. Fatima, who runs the morning crew, lays two plant tags side by side: water today and curse the temperature. Then Fatima says, A thought you cannot act on is not a task; it is weather in your head. Brooke exhales and starts with the watering cans.
examples.whatToDo: Fatima turns the worry into two tags, then sends Brooke to the task that is still hers. Brooke waters, covers, and stops refreshing the forecast.
examples.whyItMatters: A good reframe does not shame worry. It gives worry a test, and the test moves attention from the uncontrollable sky to the seedlings in reach.

examples.title: Nightstand Control Lesson

planSpec.audience: learners who confuse control sorting with giving up
planSpec.stakes: A trainee may hear the Stoic split as passivity unless confusion is used as teaching material.
planSpec.requiredBeat: The learner's confusion becomes the path into Epictetus's controllable and uncontrollable split.

examples.scenario: Armande teaches a remote onboarding lesson from a bedroom nightstand because the training room Wi-Fi is down. Teagan, the newest support hire, keeps asking why Epictetus's dichotomy of control is not just giving up. Armande points to two mugs beside the laptop: one for what a caller says, one for the controllable words Teagan chooses next. The confusion becomes the lesson.
examples.whatToDo: Armande keeps Teagan's objection on the table and turns it into a sorting drill: caller reaction in one mug, next sentence and tone in the other.
examples.whyItMatters: The teaching lands because the confusion is not brushed aside. Teagan sees that release means leaving room for conduct, not quitting on the caller.

examples.title: Lane Board Reset

planSpec.audience: competitors who turn posted rankings into mental loops
planSpec.stakes: A fixed lane assignment can either start rumination or cue the next controllable action.
planSpec.requiredBeat: The same person meets the same lane board with one variable changed: the control question.

examples.scenario: Teagan used to reach the swimming pool lane board and read every posted seed time as a verdict on her worth. One poor lane assignment would follow her into warmups. Two weeks later, she marks the board with one question: what part is mine? The lane number stays the same, but her first act changes. She checks her goggles, resets her stroke count, and lets the ranking sit on the board.
examples.whatToDo: Teagan adds one control question to the lane board ritual, then moves straight to equipment and stroke count before the ranking becomes a replay.
examples.whyItMatters: The outside fact did not improve. The variable was attention. One question changed the board from a verdict into a cue for conduct.

examples.title: Score Alert Find

planSpec.audience: clinical teams looking for hidden attention drains
planSpec.stakes: Ambient screens may be treated as harmless until work records show where attention leaked.
planSpec.requiredBeat: A quiet review of logs reveals one concrete screen-driven pattern.

examples.scenario: Hermine reviews discrepancy notes in the radiology reading room after two misses in one shift. The report times look random until she opens the room log and sees a side monitor was left on during a late game. Each addendum followed a score alert by less than a minute. The finding is small and hard to ignore: the reading room had copied sports bar televisions, only with CT scans.
examples.whatToDo: Hermine removes the side monitor from reading hours and adds a brief log note each time outside media enters the room again.
examples.whyItMatters: The audit makes distraction visible without blaming character. Once the find is concrete, the team can change the room instead of scolding focus.

examples.title: Fitting Aisle Trial

planSpec.audience: hands-on workers caught in replay while solving a physical problem
planSpec.stakes: A simple parts run can become an inner trial unless the worker returns to controllable steps.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Stay inside one person's thought process with no external dialogue.

examples.scenario: Ludovic stands at the plumbing parts shelf with a cracked valve in his palm. Wrong size. Another trip. The mind starts its usual show: angry tenant, bad review, wasted morning, boss asking why this happens to him. Wait. Which piece is mine? Part number, gasket, call back, clean note. Not the tenant's mood. Not the old mistake. He puts two fittings in the tray and leaves the rest of the trial in the aisle.
examples.whatToDo: Ludovic names the replay, keeps the repair facts, and buys the fitting that lets him act. The tenant's mood and yesterday's mistake stay off the parts list.
examples.whyItMatters: Inner noise often wears a work costume. Sorting the shelf from the trial lets Ludovic solve the pipe instead of feeding the courtroom in his head.

questions.prompt: Brooke and Fatima hear the same frost warning at the nursery table. Which response fits mental clearing best?
choices: Brooke refreshes the weather map and postpones watering until she feels calm.
Fatima marks water today, cover seedlings, and stop rehearsing frost.
Brooke asks the crew to debate every forecast so no risk is missed.
questions.explanation: The useful move is not pretending frost is pleasant. It is separating weather from duties, then doing the duties. Refreshing and debating keep the loop alive.

questions.prompt: A log on Hermine's desk shows three report pauses in ten minutes, each right after score alerts on a side screen. What should she infer first?
choices: The side screen is feeding noise before clinical choice.
The readers need a sterner reminder to care more about accuracy.
The queue should wait until everyone has read the sports scores.
questions.explanation: The pattern points to environment before character. A sports-bar-like room can refill the mind with input even when the workers are trying to be careful.

questions.prompt: At the subway map, Aanya keeps checking headlines while Ludovic traces the reachable route. Which difference matters most?
choices: Aanya has weaker focus, while Ludovic has a naturally quiet mind.
Ludovic ignores the delay, while Aanya treats the delay as serious.
Ludovic sorts delay from action, while Aanya keeps adding input.
questions.explanation: The lesson is not talent or denial. Ludovic keeps the delay in the outside pile and acts on the route, while Aanya keeps feeding the room's noise.

questions.prompt: Teagan's swim notes show the same lane result on two Fridays. The first day she replayed rankings; the second she checked goggles and stroke count. What changed?
choices: The lane board gave Teagan more encouraging information on the second Friday.
Teagan moved from outcome replay to controllable conduct.
The race became less important after she saw the same number twice.
questions.explanation: The posted result stayed outside her control. The change was Teagan's first use of attention: from ranking replay to equipment and stroke choices.

questions.prompt: Which test best catches the false calm of suppression when Armande coaches a trainee?
choices: Ask whether the thought became a duty or can be released.
Ask whether the trainee can force the thought out for one minute.
Ask whether the trainee sounds peaceful while naming the worry.
questions.explanation: Suppression measures how hard someone can push. Mental clearing asks for the claim inside the thought, then keeps only the duty it reveals.

questions.prompt: On Ludovic's repair slip, the uncontrollable column lists tenant mood and yesterday's error. The controllable column lists part number, gasket, and call back. Which next move follows?
choices: Call the tenant three times to lower the chance of anger.
Rewrite yesterday's error until the embarrassment feels useful.
Buy the fitting, make the call, and stop governing mood.
questions.explanation: The repair slip already sorted the loop. The next action belongs to the controllable column; chasing mood or old shame moves Ludovic back into rehearsal.

questions.prompt: Two responses to a bad email are on Aanya's screen: reread it until the sting fades, or write the one reply she can stand behind. Which response uses mental clearing?
choices: Write the reply she can govern, then leave the reaction alone.
Reread the email carefully enough to remove the sting before acting.
Ask a friend to guess the sender's motive before choosing any words.
questions.explanation: The reply is conduct. The sender's reaction and hidden motive are not in Aanya's hands, so rereading or guessing only gives the loop more fuel.

questions.prompt: Fatima compares two changes: hiding a news app in a folder or leaving it beside her alarm with a stricter promise. Which change fits the lesson?
choices: Leave the app visible so willpower gets more practice at night.
Keep the alarm setup and add a reminder to be disciplined.
Move the app away so the alarm stops cueing replay.
questions.explanation: Mental clearing includes changing the room. A stricter promise leaves the cue in place, while moving the app makes the default mistake harder.

questions.prompt: Hermine tells a resident that mental clearing means making the mind blank. What correction should the resident make?
choices: Treat blankness as the goal and use pressure to hold it.
Call it room for perception and the next act.
Replace hard thoughts with pleasant scenes until the shift ends.
questions.explanation: Blankness is the false target. The mind needs room to see and choose; pleasant replacement can become another loop if it avoids duty.

reviewCards.front: What does Epictetus's dichotomy of control help you sort?
reviewCards.back: It separates what you can govern, such as attention, judgment, words, and conduct, from what drains you without taking orders from you.

reviewCards.front: How is mental clearing different from forcing a blank mind?
reviewCards.back: Forcing blankness fights thought directly. Mental clearing listens for any duty inside the thought, acts on what is controllable, and stops feeding the rest.

reviewCards.front: Earlier concept, Limit Your Inputs: how does it pair with mental clearing?
reviewCards.back: Limiting inputs turns down fresh noise from feeds, screens, and alerts. Mental clearing also handles the loops already inside by sorting them into control and release.

reviewCards.front: Earlier concept, Become Present: what does presence reveal before clearing starts?
reviewCards.back: Presence lets you notice the live object in front of you: the person, tool, breath, or task. That notice shows which thought is pulling you away.

reviewCards.front: Why can a sports bar dinner keep working on the mind after you leave?
reviewCards.back: The room trains attention to graze across screens. Later, the body may be elsewhere while the mind keeps replaying headlines, scores, and arguments it never chose.

reviewCards.front: What are the three steps in Sort the Control Queue?
reviewCards.back: Name the loop, mark it controllable or uncontrollable, then return to conduct. If the thought has no next act, refuse to rehearse it again.

implementationPlan.title: Sort the Control Queue
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice catching one thought loop before it becomes the room you live in. Sort the Control Queue by naming the loop, marking it controllable or uncontrollable, then doing the next conduct step. If the loop has no step, stop feeding it with more input.

ifThenPlans.context: A screen is open beside a meal, meeting, or bed.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the screen is cueing extra noise, then Sort the Control Queue: close or move it, name what you came to do, and return to that person or task.

ifThenPlans.context: An old argument starts replaying while you work.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the argument starts another lap, then write the one repair you can make. If there is no repair, label it outside control and resume the task.

ifThenPlans.context: A future outcome keeps asking for another forecast.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the forecast loop repeats, then name the next conduct step, do that step, and leave the outcome out of the work area.

ifThenPlans.context: You catch yourself trying to crush a thought.
ifThenPlans.plan: If force becomes the method, then stop and ask what claim the thought is making. Keep a real duty; release the rehearsal.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next 24 hours, Sort the Control Queue on three loops. Write the loop, mark controllable or uncontrollable, and take one conduct step or release it.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For seven days, adjust one environment each evening: move one feed, screen, or alert away from the place where loops begin, then note which loop lost fuel.

memorableLines.text: If a thought cannot lead to conduct, it does not get the chair.
memorableLines.why: It turns control sorting into a picture the reader can use.

memorableLines.text: A clear mind is a workbench, not a vacant lot.
memorableLines.why: It prevents stillness from sounding like blankness.

memorableLines.text: Suppression gives the thought a wrestling partner.
memorableLines.why: It makes the hard edge against force easy to remember.
